title: Stablecoins Are Becoming Financial Infrastructure — Not Just Crypto Infrastructure
description: Stablecoins have moved from a crypto-trading tool to real payment rails for remittances, payroll, and treasury. Here's what changed, and what hasn't.
excerpt: For most of the past decade, a stablecoin — a cryptocurrency engineered to hold a steady value, typically pegged one-to-one to a fiat currency like the U.S. dollar — existed for one reason: to let traders move in and out of volatile crypto assets without cashing out to a bank account every time. That was the job. It was a trading tool, not a financial system. That framing is out of date. Fintechs are routing cross-border payroll through stablecoin rails. Payment processors are piloting stablecoin settlement to cut the multi-day delay of correspondent banking. Corporate treasury teams — the same people who obsess over overnight interest rates — are asking whether holding a slice of working capital in a regulated stablecoin makes operational sense. None of that is trading. That's infrastructure. From trading pairs to plumbing The shift didn't happen because stablecoins got more exciting. It happened because the boring case got stronger. A dollar-pegged token that settles on a public blockchain moves the same way at 2 a.m. on a Sunday as it does at 10 a.m. on a Tuesday — the network doesn't know the difference. Traditional cross-border payments, by contrast, still route through a chain of correspondent banks, each with its own cutoff times, holidays, and compliance checks. For a business paying contractors in a dozen countries, that gap in speed and predictability is a real cost, not a technical curiosity. Proponents of stablecoin settlement point to same-day or near-instant finality versus a process that can take several business days through legacy rails. That comparison is doing a lot of work in every pitch deck about stablecoins right now, and it's worth treating as a claim to verify against your own use case rather than a universal truth — settlement speed on-chain doesn't eliminate the off-ramp friction of converting back to local currency at the other end, which is often where the real delay and cost still live. Why banks stopped pretending not to notice A few years ago, the standard line from large banks was that stablecoins were a niche crypto product with no relevance to regulated finance. That line has quietly disappeared. Card networks have explored stablecoin settlement for merchant payouts. Custody banks have built stablecoin-adjacent products. None of this is charity — it's defensive positioning. If a meaningful share of cross-border value starts moving over stablecoin rails, the institutions that sat it out lose a fee-generating layer of the payments stack they've owned for decades. title: Ethereum vs. Solana: What Are Developers Actually Building On?
description: A practical look at where developers actually build — DeFi, tokenization, consumer apps — and the tradeoffs that drive the choice between Ethereum and Solana.
excerpt: Every crypto cycle produces a version of the same argument: which layer-1 (L1) blockchain — a base network that processes and finalizes its own transactions, rather than relying on another chain for security — is "winning." It's a framing built for price charts, not for the people who actually have to choose a chain to build a product on. Developers don't pick a network because of what it did last quarter. They pick it because of what it lets them ship this quarter, and Ethereum and Solana have genuinely different answers to that question. Ethereum: depth over speed Ethereum's advantage has never really been raw transaction speed — it's the depth and maturity of what's already built on top of it. The largest concentration of decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols, the most established smart contract tooling (smart contracts being self-executing code that runs on a blockchain without a central operator), and the biggest ecosystem of layer-2 (L2) networks — scaling chains that process transactions off Ethereum's main chain but settle back to it for security — all live here. For a team building something that needs to plug into existing lending markets, decentralized exchanges, or tokenized real-world assets, Ethereum and its L2 ecosystem is usually where the liquidity and the composability — the ability for protocols to plug into each other like software libraries — already exist. That depth comes at a cost: Ethereum's own base layer can get expensive and congested during heavy usage, which is precisely why the L2 rollup ecosystem exists in the first place — to inherit Ethereum's security while processing transactions more cheaply elsewhere. The tradeoff for builders is added complexity: deciding which L2 to deploy on, and how to think about liquidity that's now spread across a dozen different networks instead of concentrated on one chain. Solana: one chain, high throughput Solana took the opposite architectural bet: rather than scaling through a constellation of L2s, keep everything on one high-throughput base layer designed from the ground up for speed and low transaction cost. That design has made Solana a default choice for products where a user is expected to transact frequently and cheaply — decentralized exchanges built for active trading, consumer payment apps, gaming, and social applications where charging a meaningful fee per click would kill the product. title: Why Wall Street Keeps Launching Crypto Exchange-Traded Funds
description: What asset managers keep launching crypto ETFs for, what an ETF wrapper gives up versus holding crypto directly, and what it signals about adoption.
excerpt: Once regulators in major markets began approving spot crypto exchange-traded funds — ETFs, meaning funds that trade on a stock exchange like a share of stock but hold an underlying asset, in this case crypto, directly — asset managers didn't file one or two and wait to see how it went. They kept filing. New wrappers, new baskets, new structures, from firms that spent years publicly skeptical of crypto as an asset class. That pattern is less about a sudden conversion to crypto conviction and more about how the fund business actually works. The business logic is simple Asset managers make money on fees collected as a percentage of assets under management. A new ETF category with real, sustained investor demand — the kind spot Bitcoin and Ether funds demonstrated — is a rare thing in an industry where most new fund launches attract limited assets. Once one firm proves a category works, competitors face a straightforward choice: launch a competing product and fight for a share of that fee pool, or cede the category entirely to whoever got there first. Most large firms chose the former, which is the simplest explanation for why the field kept getting crowded even as the flagship products matured. What a crypto ETF actually replaces The pitch to a traditional investor is straightforward: exposure to a crypto asset's price through a brokerage account they already have, with no need to set up a separate crypto exchange account, manage a digital wallet, or safeguard a private key — the cryptographic credential that controls access to crypto held directly. For an investor who's decided they want price exposure and nothing else, that's a meaningful reduction in operational complexity and a set of self-custody risks removed entirely. What it doesn't replicate is anything that requires actually holding the underlying asset on-chain. An ETF holder generally isn't eligible for staking rewards — yield earned by participating in a proof-of-stake network's validation process — and has no ability to use the asset directly in decentralized applications, vote in on-chain governance, or move it peer-to-peer. It's also only tradable when the exchange it's listed on is open, while the underlying crypto asset itself trades continuously. Investors weighing a crypto ETF against direct ownership are really deciding how much of that on-chain functionality they actually plan to use. title: Crypto Wallets Are Getting Easier to Use. Is the Seed Phrase Era Ending?
description: How account abstraction, passkeys, and social recovery are replacing the seed phrase as crypto wallets' default onboarding experience, and the tradeoffs.
excerpt: Ask anyone who's tried to get a non-technical friend into crypto what the actual barrier was, and the answer is rarely the technology of blockchains themselves. It's the seed phrase — a sequence of 12 or 24 words generated when a wallet is created, which serves as the master backup for every private key that wallet controls. Lose it, and the funds are gone permanently, with no customer service line to call. Write it down wrong, store it somewhere insecure, or get tricked into typing it into a fake website, and the outcome is the same. It is, by design, unforgiving — and that design has been the single biggest onboarding failure point in the industry's history. Why it was ever built this way The seed phrase exists because of a core principle: self-custody, meaning the user — not an exchange, not a bank, not any company — holds the private key that actually controls their funds. That principle is a large part of what makes crypto crypto. The problem is that pure self-custody puts the entire burden of security on one human being with no institutional safety net, which is a reasonable tradeoff for a security researcher and a brutal one for someone's first week in the space. What's replacing the seed phrase Several overlapping approaches are converging on the same goal: keep the self-custody principle, remove the single-point-of-failure string of words. Account abstraction turns a wallet into a smart contract with programmable rules, rather than a private key with no logic attached — enabling features like spending limits, multi-step approval for large transactions, and recovery methods that don't depend on a single secret. Passkeys let a wallet be secured with the same biometric or device-based authentication — fingerprint, face recognition, device PIN — that already secures most people's phones and password managers, instead of a phrase they have to store separately. Social recovery allows a user to designate a small group of trusted contacts or devices who can collectively help restore wallet access if the primary device is lost, without any single one of them being able to move funds alone. Multi-party computation (MPC) wallets split the key material itself across multiple devices or parties, so no single device ever holds a complete private key that could be lost or stolen in one shot. title: What Is a Blockchain Node — and Why Does Decentralization Depend on Them?
description: A plain-English explainer on what a blockchain node is, how it differs from a validator or miner, and why node count and distribution drive decentralization.
excerpt: "Decentralized" is one of the most used and least examined words in crypto. Every network claims it. Almost nobody explains what it actually rests on. The honest answer is unglamorous: decentralization is a function of nodes — how many independently operated computers are running a network's software, verifying its rules, and refusing to go along with anything that breaks them. What a node actually does A blockchain node is a computer running software that keeps a copy of the network's ledger and enforces its rules. In practical terms, a full node does three things continuously: it validates incoming transactions against the network's rules — rejecting anything that tries to spend funds that don't exist or breaks a protocol rule — it relays valid transactions and blocks to other nodes it's connected to, and it keeps its own copy of the ledger's history up to date. A node doesn't take anyone's word for it. It checks the rules itself, independently, every time. Node, validator, miner — the difference These terms get used loosely and it causes real confusion. A full node stores a complete copy of the ledger and independently verifies everything against the network's rules; running one doesn't require staking any capital. A light node does a scaled-down version of the same job, trusting full nodes for some data rather than verifying every detail itself, in exchange for needing far less storage and bandwidth. A validator is a specific role in proof-of-stake networks — the operator stakes (locks up) a meaningful amount of the network's token as collateral and, in exchange, gets the right to propose and confirm new blocks, earning rewards and risking penalties for misbehavior. A miner is the equivalent role in proof-of-work networks like Bitcoin, competing to solve a computational puzzle to add the next block. Every validator and every miner is running node software, but plenty of nodes are neither — they're just quietly verifying and relaying, which is exactly the point. Why the count and the spread matter more than the total A network with ten thousand nodes that are almost all rented from the same two cloud computing providers is, in a meaningful sense, less decentralized than a smaller network whose nodes are spread across many independent operators, hardware setups, and countries. title: Tokenization Is Growing Fast. Does Everything Really Need a Token?
description: What tokenization actually adds versus a normal database, when putting an asset on-chain solves a real problem, and when it's a token for its own sake.
excerpt: Tokenization — representing an asset, a right, or a piece of data as a digital token on a blockchain — is one of the most consistently hyped ideas in crypto, and unlike a lot of hype cycles, this one has some genuinely strong use cases underneath it. It also has an enormous amount of noise sitting on top of those use cases, and the two are getting harder to tell apart the faster the category grows. The real use cases Some categories of tokenization solve a specific, verifiable problem that's hard to solve any other way. Real-world asset (RWA) tokenization of instruments like government treasuries or bonds can enable fractional ownership and near-instant settlement between parties who'd otherwise be stuck in slow, paperwork-heavy transfer processes. Supply-chain and provenance tracking — recording each step an asset takes from origin to final buyer directly on a shared, tamper-resistant ledger — gives every participant in the chain the same verifiable record instead of each company keeping its own unverifiable spreadsheet. Charitable giving is a similar case: an on-chain donation trail lets a donor verify that funds moved where they were promised, which is a transparency problem traditional nonprofit accounting has struggled with for a long time. What these use cases share is a common thread: the token isn't decoration. It's doing something a normal database couldn't do as well — giving multiple parties who don't fully trust each other a shared, independently verifiable record, without a single company controlling and potentially altering that record. The token-for-token's-sake problem Then there's the much larger category: products that added a token because a token is a fundraising mechanism and a growth hack, not because the product needed one. The tell is usually simple — remove the token, and does the actual product stop working, or does only the price chart disappear? A loyalty-points program that could run perfectly well as rows in a company's existing database doesn't automatically get better by becoming a token; it gets a speculative price attached to it, which is a different thing entirely and, for a lot of these products, actually works against the stated purpose by turning a simple rewards mechanic into something people trade instead of use. title: The Senate Votes on the CLARITY Act Tomorrow. It Should Pass.
description: The Senate holds a cloture vote on the CLARITY Act. ChainBrief makes the case for passage: the roadblocks, the key senators, and what betting markets price in.
excerpt: Editorial: this is a ChainBrief.news opinion piece, reflecting our own editorial judgment on pending legislation — not a straight news report, and not legal or financial advice. Our news coverage and our opinion pages are produced separately. At 2:15 p.m. ET on Tuesday, the Senate holds a cloture vote on the motion to proceed to the CLARITY Act — formally the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act. It is not a vote on final passage. It's a procedural vote to end debate and let the Senate actually take up a bill that would, for the first time, give the United States a real statutory answer to a question that has hung over the crypto industry for a decade: which federal regulator is actually in charge. Clearing it takes 60 votes. Republicans hold 53 seats. They need at least seven Democrats to cross over, and as of this writing that math is not locked in. We think the Senate should clear it. Not because the bill is perfect — it isn't, and we'll get to exactly where it falls short — but because the alternative on offer isn't a better bill. It's more of the same regulatory limbo that has already pushed companies, jobs, and enforcement clarity offshore, with no serious replacement plan waiting in the wings if this vote fails. What tomorrow's vote actually is As Senator Bernie Moreno (R-OH), one of the bill's floor advocates, put it ahead of the vote: this is “not a vote on final passage. If the Senate does pass its own version, it would still need to be reconciled with the market structure bill the House already passed in July 2025 before anything reaches the president's desk. Tomorrow is a gate, not a finish line — but it's the gate the bill has been stuck behind for months, after the Senate adjourned for its summer break in August without taking it up. title: Circle Built Its Own Blockchain. The Gas Token Is USDC.
description: Circle's Arc layer-1 launched with USDC as its gas token, a permissioned validator set including BlackRock and DTCC, and sub-second finality. Here's why.
excerpt: On September 16, Circle — the company behind USDC, the second-largest dollar-pegged stablecoin — launched Arc, its own layer-1 (L1) blockchain, on mainnet. The timing is hard to read as coincidence: one day earlier, the Senate had failed to clear a cloture vote on the CLARITY Act, the bill that would have given digital assets a clear federal jurisdictional line. While Washington's attempt at a public framework stalled, one of the industry's largest stablecoin issuers quietly finished building a private one. What makes Arc different Arc's core design choice is that USDC itself is the network's native gas token — every transaction fee is paid, and denominated, in dollars, rather than a separate volatile network asset the way ETH or SOL function on Ethereum and Solana. Fee pricing is set by a weighted moving average of network demand rather than adjusting block to block, which is aimed squarely at giving institutional users a predictable cost rather than a speculative one. Consensus runs on Malachite , a Byzantine fault-tolerant engine derived from Tendermint, which Circle says delivers deterministic finality in well under a second — a transaction is either final the moment its block closes, or it isn't, with none of the probabilistic "wait a few more confirmations to be safe" behavior that networks like Ethereum and Bitcoin rely on. The execution layer is built on Reth and is fully EVM-compatible, so existing Solidity contracts and standard Ethereum tooling deploy on Arc largely unmodified. It also ships with an optional privacy layer that can shield transfer amounts — a feature aimed directly at institutions that need to settle on a shared ledger without broadcasting position sizes to competitors. Who's actually running it This is the part that separates Arc from almost every other L1 launch: its validator set isn't open. title: Five Utility Tokens, Put to the Test
description: A skeptical, test-based look at five utility tokens — Chainlink, Filecoin, Helium, Render, Livepeer — asking whether each actually needs a token.
excerpt: Round-ups of "utility tokens to watch" are a genre unto themselves, and most of them share the same structural flaw: they pick projects with a working product, then work backward to explain why the token attached to it is meaningful. We wanted to try the opposite. In an earlier piece on tokenization, we proposed a three-question test for cutting through the hype: does the token need multiple parties who don't fully trust each other to share a verifiable record, rather than one company's database? Does removing the token break the actual product, or just the price chart? And is the underlying process genuinely illiquid or opaque today in a way a token fixes? Here's five tokens run through that test, plainly, with no attempt to make all five come out looking the same. Chainlink (LINK) — passes Chainlink's oracle network feeds external, real-world data — prices, weather, sports results, proof of reserves — onto blockchains that otherwise have no native way to know anything happening off-chain. The token secures the network: node operators stake LINK as collateral they lose if they report bad data, which is a genuinely different trust model than a single company's data feed. Remove the token, and the economic incentive that makes operators accountable for accuracy disappears with it — this isn't a database with a price chart bolted on; the token is doing real work, and a large share of on-chain DeFi activity depends on oracle data actually being reliable. title: What Is a Cloture? And Is the CLARITY Act Dead, or Dead for Now?
description: A plain-English explainer on Senate cloture: why the CLARITY Act needed 60 votes, what happens after a failed vote, and whether the bill is really dead.
excerpt: When the CLARITY Act's cloture vote failed 49-50 on September 15, plenty of the reaction treated it as the Senate voting the bill down. That's not quite what happened. The Senate didn't vote on the CLARITY Act's merits that day — it voted on whether to end debate and let itself formally consider the bill at all. Understanding why that distinction matters means understanding cloture, one of the most consequential and least understood mechanics in American lawmaking. What cloture actually is Cloture is the Senate's formal procedure, under Rule XXII, for ending debate on a pending matter so the chamber can move to an actual vote. It exists because Senate rules otherwise let debate continue indefinitely — the mechanism behind the filibuster — meaning a determined minority can block a bill from ever reaching a final vote simply by refusing to stop talking about it, or refusing to agree to stop. For most legislation, invoking cloture requires the support of three-fifths of senators duly chosen and sworn — 60 votes out of 100, assuming no vacancies — a materially higher bar than the simple majority that decides the bill itself once debate actually ends. Why this needed 60 votes, not 51 The September 15 vote specifically was cloture on the motion to proceed — the procedural step of formally bringing the bill to the floor, which is itself subject to a filibuster and its own cloture requirement, separate from the cloture vote and final passage vote that would still be needed on the bill itself further down the road. It's common, on major legislation, for the Senate to need cloture invoked two or three separate times before a bill reaches final passage — once to proceed to the bill, potentially again on amendments, and again on passage itself. The CLARITY Act didn't clear the first of those hurdles. What happens when cloture succeeds Had the vote passed, the Senate would have moved into a strict, rules-bound phase: a hard cap of 30 hours of further debate on legislation, with no senator allowed more than one hour of floor time, and only amendments filed before the cloture vote and ruled germane eligible for consideration — no new amendments once the clock starts. That's the tradeoff cloture makes: harder to invoke, but once invoked, it guarantees the chamber actually reaches a vote instead of debating forever. title: Aave, Morpho, and Uniswap Just Deployed on a Chain They Don't Control
description: DeFi protocols including Aave and Morpho deployed on Circle's permissioned Arc blockchain at launch. Here's why, and the tension with DeFi's permissionless roots.

More than a hundred applications reportedly deployed alongside it on day one, including an Aave V4 market, Morpho, and Uniswap-adjacent infrastructure, plus a dozen major exchanges routing order flow its way. That's a genuinely unusual amount of coordinated day-one liquidity for a brand-new L1. title: Why 18 State Attorneys General — Republicans and Democrats Alike — Wanted CLARITY Dead
description: An explainer on the bipartisan 18-state coalition that opposed CLARITY over federal preemption, the disputed 'qualified transaction' definition, and the stakes.
excerpt: Most of the coverage of the CLARITY Act's failure focused on the ethics fight over the Trump family's crypto business, or the stablecoin-rewards dispute between banks and crypto firms. A quieter objection got less national attention despite coming from an unusually bipartisan coalition: eighteen state attorneys general, led by New York's Letitia James and including Republican Kris Kobach and Democrat Rob Bonta among the signatories, sent the Senate a letter urging it to reject the bill outright over federal preemption. The core claim: "qualified transaction" The AGs' objection centers on a specific phrase in the bill's text: its definition of a "qualified transaction." Their letter argues that definition would let the SEC's federal framework preempt state securities and commodities enforcement over transactions that would otherwise fall under state authority — meaning a state attorney general trying to bring a fraud case against a crypto platform could find a defendant arguing that federal law already occupies that ground, regardless of whether the SEC actually brought its own case. The "reserved" language fig leaf More recent drafts of the bill added language the AGs describe as "reserving" certain state fraud-prosecution powers — an attempt to address exactly this concern. The coalition's response was that the reservation language is too vague to rely on in practice: as the letter put it, they "remain firmly opposed to any federal statutory changes that would displace states' authority to oversee the securities and commodities markets," arguing that ambiguous statutory language is precisely the kind of thing that reads fine in a press release and collapses the first time a well-resourced defendant's legal team tests it in court. “We remain firmly opposed to any federal statutory changes that would displace states' authority to oversee the securities and commodities markets.” — from the eighteen state attorneys general’s letter to the Senate The stakes they cited The letter leaned on FBI figures putting crypto-related fraud losses at $11.4 billion in a single year to argue for why the preemption question isn't academic. title: The SEC Just Let Real Stocks Trade on Public Blockchains
description: The SEC granted a five-year exemption letting real, dividend- and voting-rights-bearing U.S. shares trade on public blockchains. The mechanism, and who benefits.
excerpt: On September 17, the SEC granted a five-year exemptive-relief framework that lets tokenized U.S. stocks trade directly on automated market makers (AMMs) — decentralized trading venues that price assets algorithmically instead of matching buy and sell orders the way a traditional exchange does — running on public blockchains including Ethereum, Solana, and BNB Chain. The venues don't have to register as securities exchanges to do it. This isn't the synthetic "stock token" model some platforms have offered for years, where a derivative tracks a share's price without conferring any actual ownership. The SEC's order requires real shares, carrying real dividend and voting rights, represented on-chain. How the exemption actually works Exemptive relief is a specific SEC tool: rather than writing a new rule through the full notice-and-comment process, the agency uses existing statutory authority to exempt a defined activity from requirements that would otherwise apply — in this case, exchange registration. It's the same general mechanism the SEC has used before to let novel financial products operate ahead of, or instead of, a full rulemaking (spot ETFs are a familiar example). That makes this framework flexible and fast to issue, but also less durable than a statute: a future SEC could narrow or revoke it without needing Congress. The guardrails The relief isn't unconditional. Trading venues have to notify a company 30 days before its shares begin trading on-chain, and the company can object and block participation — an issuer veto that doesn't exist for ordinary secondary-market trading of a stock today. Venues also have to run know-your-customer (KYC) checks, apply trading limits, and layer permissioned access controls on top of what are otherwise open, permissionless blockchains. In practice, that means the underlying settlement layer is public, but who can actually trade isn't — a hybrid that regulators clearly designed to keep AML and investor-protection obligations intact rather than exporting them to code. Who's positioned to benefit — and who's shut out Tokenization platforms including Securitize, Bullish, Superstate, Dinari, and Fairmint are positioned to build the compliant rails this framework requires. Coinbase and Robinhood, both of which already run brokerage infrastructure, are expected to have a head start adapting to it. title: The CFTC Sent Its Crypto Rulebook to the White House. Here's What That Actually Means.
description: The CFTC submitted a crypto market-structure proposal to the White House OMB after the Senate's failed CLARITY vote. What the submission means, and what's next.
excerpt: On September 18 — three days after the Senate failed to clear cloture on the CLARITY Act — the CFTC submitted a new crypto market-structure proposal to the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review. It's a procedural step, not a finished rule, but it's a meaningful one: it confirms the CFTC isn't waiting on Congress and is moving through the rulemaking machinery it already has. What "sent to OMB" actually means Federal agencies don't just publish a new rule the moment they write one. A "significant" regulatory action typically goes through interagency review — commonly through OMB's Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs — before the agency can formally propose it. After that review, the CFTC's own reporting indicates the proposal returns to the agency for a commissioner vote, then a public comment period, then another vote before it can take effect. In plain terms: this is an early step in a multi-stage process, not a rule taking effect next week. What's actually in the proposal — and what isn't public yet The specifics haven't been disclosed. It's not yet public which crypto assets the proposal would cover, what registration or disclosure requirements exchanges would face, or how far the CFTC is reaching under its existing authority over commodity derivatives. That's worth naming plainly rather than guessing at: the headline here is that the CFTC moved, not yet what it decided. “The CFTC is locked in and ready to ship its rules for the new frontier of finance,” CFTC Chair Mike Selig said following the submission. A second, smaller move the same week Separately, the CFTC issued no-action relief allowing certain passive software providers — including crypto wallet interfaces — to connect users to regulated derivatives markets without registering as introducing brokers. It's a narrower move than the market-structure proposal, but it points the same direction: the agency easing its own registration requirements where it can, rather than waiting for new statutory categories from Congress. title: A Hacker Drained $319 Million From a Bitcoin Network, Then Gave Most of It Back
description: A caching bug let an attacker mint unbacked bitcoin and withdraw $319 million from Liquid Network. About 85% came back after a patch. Here's what happened.
excerpt: On September 6, an attacker exploited a bug in Liquid Network — a Bitcoin sidechain built by Blockstream that more than 80 exchanges and infrastructure firms use as a faster settlement layer — to mint roughly 4,000 bitcoin that weren't actually backed by any reserve, then withdraw about $319 million of it through an approved trading platform called SideSwap. The whole sequence, from the first malformed transaction to the payout leaving the network, took about 36 minutes. How a sidechain works, and how this broke it Liquid issues a token called L-BTC, meant to be backed one-to-one by real bitcoin held in a multi-institution reserve called the federation wallet — the idea being that L-BTC settles faster than bitcoin's own base chain while staying redeemable for the real thing. The bug lived in Elements, the open-source software Liquid runs on: nodes cache the results of range-proof checks, a cryptographic step that verifies a transaction's amounts are valid, to save on repeated computation. A flaw in that caching let at least one invalid output pass as already-verified — effectively letting the attacker mint L-BTC without putting up real bitcoin behind it. Blockstream confirmed this was a software bug, not a stolen private key or a breached wallet. The conditional return The attacker communicated on-chain, describing themselves as a "whitehat" and telling Blockstream, in effect: fix the bug first, and the money comes back once the fix is confirmed. Liquid halted all transactions while the federation worked on a patch. After it shipped, the attacker returned about 3,400 BTC — roughly 85% of what was taken, worth about $272 million — and kept the remaining 598 BTC, worth around $47 million. “Please fix the bug first... Then we will transfer the money back safely after confirming the fix,” the attacker wrote in an on-chain message. What's still unresolved Blockstream hasn't detailed how it plans to cover the roughly $47 million shortfall the attacker kept, or when full redemptions will fully resume for L-BTC holders. Reconstructions of the federation's reserve after the returned funds put the implied backing ratio somewhere around 86% against outstanding L-BTC — not fully reconciled, and not the one-to-one peg the token is supposed to guarantee. Liquid has since resumed operations. title: What Is "Exemptive Relief," and Why Is the SEC Using It Instead of Writing New Rules?
description: A plain-language explainer on SEC exemptive relief: what it is, how it differs from rulemaking, its history with products like ETFs, and why it's everywhere now.
excerpt: When the SEC let tokenized U.S. stocks trade on public blockchains this month, it didn't do it by passing a law, and it didn't do it through a full formal rulemaking either. It used something called exemptive relief — a tool that's been part of securities regulation for decades, and one that's showing up constantly in crypto policy coverage right now without much explanation of what it actually is. The basic idea Securities law bars certain activities by default unless an exception applies. Exemptive relief is the SEC using authority Congress already gave it — typically under specific provisions of the securities and investment-company statutes — to grant an exception for a defined activity, usually with conditions attached. It's not the agency ignoring the law; it's the agency using a tool the law explicitly built in for situations that don't fit neatly into existing categories. How it's different from a full rulemaking A formal SEC rule normally goes through notice-and-comment rulemaking: the agency proposes a rule, the public gets a window to submit comments, the agency responds to those comments, and only then does a final rule take effect. That process is designed to be thorough, and it's also slow — often taking many months or longer for anything contentious. Exemptive relief, by contrast, can be granted directly by the Commission for a specific applicant or a defined class of activity, without the same extended public process. It trades some of that deliberative rigor for speed. Where this tool has been used before This isn't new. Some of the SEC's more consequential market structure has actually run on exemptive relief rather than dedicated legislation — exchange-traded funds themselves operated for years under a patchwork of individual exemptive orders before the SEC eventually adopted a generalized rule covering most ETFs. The pattern is familiar: a new product type doesn't fit the existing rulebook, the SEC grants exemptions to let it operate while it studies the space, and a more permanent rule sometimes follows years later — sometimes it doesn't, and the exemption regime just continues. The tradeoff nobody should skip past Speed comes at a cost: durability. A statute passed by Congress is comparatively hard to unwind — it takes another act of Congress. An exemptive order is a Commission-level decision, which means a differently composed Commission, under a different administration, can revisit it. Tokenized equities specifically are up 390.4% year-to-date, the fastest-growing category by far, helped along by the SEC's new exemptive-relief framework letting real shares trade on public blockchains. Both of those numbers are real. So is a third one that gets left out of most of the celebratory coverage: even at $34 billion, tokenized assets represent roughly 0.01% of the estimated $300 trillion in traditional assets they're theoretically capable of representing. Where the money actually is Bonds and money-market instruments dominate the category, at $18.29 billion — 53.5% of the entire RWA market — though that's still only about 0.017% of the global bond and money-market universe. Tokenized equities have grown the fastest but remain the smallest major slice in absolute terms, at $4.43 billion against a $151.9 trillion global listed-equity market — 0.003% penetration. Across the RWA market broadly, only about 12% of tokenized capital is active on-chain in any meaningful sense — deployed into lending markets, liquidity pools, or collateral, rather than just sitting as a static token representing an off-chain asset. For tokenized equities specifically, that "capital activation rate" sits at 7.54%, with most of the active share concentrated in liquidity pools (65.4%) and lending protocols (28.1%). title: Staking Finally Showed Up Inside a U.S. Crypto ETF
description: Grayscale's Ethereum ETF began distributing staking rewards, a first for a U.S.-listed spot crypto fund. Canary Capital has filed a staked SEI ETF too.
excerpt: For as long as U.S. spot crypto ETFs have existed, they've had a structural gap compared to actually holding the underlying asset yourself: an investor holding Ethereum directly can stake it and earn a yield for helping secure the network, but a fund simply holding ETH in cold storage couldn't pass that yield through to shareholders. That gap started closing when Grayscale enabled staking for its Ethereum products in October 2025, and it became visible in dollar terms in January 2026, when the Grayscale Ethereum Staking ETF made its first distribution — $0.083178 per share, covering rewards earned between October and December 2025. Why this took as long as it did Staking isn't just "holding" an asset — it means locking it into a network's validation process, which introduces operational questions a passive custody arrangement doesn't have: which validator does the fund's ETH get staked through, what happens if that validator is penalized ("slashed") for misbehavior, and how does the fund handle the unstaking delay if it needs to meet redemptions. Those are legitimate structural questions, not just regulatory foot-dragging, and they're the reason staking inside a U.S.-listed ETF wrapper took meaningfully longer to arrive than the ETFs themselves. “Distributing staking rewards to ETHE shareholders is a landmark moment, not just for Grayscale, but for the entire Ethereum community,” Grayscale CEO Peter Mintzberg said. title: Wall Street Found a Way Into Prediction Markets Without Touching the Bets Themselves
description: ETF provider Tema launched a fund holding equity stakes in Kalshi and Polymarket rather than their contracts, sidestepping ongoing SEC scrutiny.
excerpt: ETF provider Tema recently launched a fund built around the prediction-markets sector's growth — with a structural choice that's more interesting than the fund itself. Roughly 15% of the fund's holdings are stakes in Kalshi and Polymarket, the privately held companies that operate the two largest prediction-market platforms. What the fund explicitly doesn't hold is exposure to the actual event contracts — the yes/no bets on elections, economic data, or other outcomes that Kalshi and Polymarket are best known for. Those remain tied up in an ongoing SEC review of whether, and how, such contracts should be regulated. The regulatory question this sidesteps Prediction-market contracts sit in a genuinely unsettled place: are they commodity derivatives regulated by the CFTC, are they something closer to securities, or are they closer to the state-regulated gaming and betting markets they resemble in function? That question hasn't been resolved, which is exactly why a fund can't simply hold event contracts directly without taking on that regulatory uncertainty itself. Owning equity in the companies is a different, better-understood legal category — regular corporate stock — even though the companies' underlying business is exactly the contested activity. Why this is a genuinely clever structure It's worth naming the mechanism plainly: this is regulatory arbitrage, not a loophole being exploited in bad faith. The fund gives investors exposure to prediction markets' growth — trading volume, revenue, user growth — without the fund itself having to take a position on how individual event contracts should be classified. If Kalshi and Polymarket's underlying business grows, the companies' value should reflect that, which is the exposure the fund is actually selling, whatever the SEC eventually decides about the contracts themselves. That visibility is part of what's driving investor interest broadly, distinct from the specific regulatory question the SEC is weighing. title: The Fed Just Wrote the Actual Rulebook for Stablecoins
description: The Fed proposed capital, reserve, and two-day redemption rules for GENIUS Act stablecoin issuers — the operational detail behind the 2026 law.
excerpt: On September 24, the Federal Reserve proposed the rules that will actually govern how a payment stablecoin issuer operates under the GENIUS Act — the federal stablecoin law that takes effect January 18, 2027, or 120 days after final implementing rules, whichever comes first. The law itself said issuers need to hold reserves and be capable of redeeming stablecoins at par. This proposal is where "capable of" turns into specific numbers. The headline number is a tiered capital charge: 2% of an issuer's first $20 billion in stablecoins outstanding, 1.5% of the next $30 billion, and 1% of anything above $50 billion, on top of separate charges tied to credit and operational risk. Read that closely and the structure is regressive by design — the marginal capital requirement gets lighter as an issuer gets bigger. For a company the size of Circle or Tether, that's a meaningful economic difference between the proposal that shipped and one that charged a flat percentage across the board. What happens if the reserve math doesn't add up The redemption mechanics are the part with real teeth. Issuers must process redemptions within two business days — fast enough to matter in a stress scenario, but not instant, which is itself a signal that regulators don't expect stablecoins to behave like bank deposits with same-day ATM withdrawals. If an issuer's reserves fall below full backing, it has to notify the Fed immediately and do one of two things: restore reserves through an approved remediation plan, or liquidate and redeem the outstanding stablecoins. There's no third option where a shortfall just sits there. Issuers also have to publish monthly reports on outstanding stablecoins and reserve composition, and those reports need sign-off from a registered public accountant plus certification from the issuer's own CEO and CFO. That's a meaningfully higher bar than the voluntary attestations most stablecoin issuers currently publish — it puts named executives on the hook the same way Sarbanes-Oxley put corporate officers on the hook for financial statements. A separate track for banks Alongside the capital and redemption rules, the Fed published a second, related proposal covering how Fed-supervised banks apply for approval to issue payment stablecoins through subsidiaries. That matters because it's a different regulatory path than the one used by crypto-native issuers seeking OCC trust charters — ChainBrief covered the OCC's own charter track for firms like Circle and Crypto.com separately. title: The SEC's Quiet End-Run Around a Stalled Congress
description: The SEC proposed "Regulation Crypto Assets," a securities-law framework with new offering exemptions and a safe harbor — built without waiting on Congress.
excerpt: On August 18, the SEC proposed a rule it's calling Regulation Crypto Assets — and the timing tells you most of what you need to know about it. The Senate had already failed to pass the CLARITY Act's cloture vote, and rather than wait for Congress to try again, the SEC built a crypto-specific framework out of authority it already holds under the existing Securities Act. The proposal doesn't touch trading venues or custody standards — that's left to the CFTC or a future rulemaking. What it does cover is capital formation: how a crypto project can legally raise money from U.S. investors without running the multi-year, multi-million-dollar gauntlet of a full securities registration. Two new ways to raise money The rule creates two registration exemptions sized for very different companies. One allows up to $5 million in token offerings over a four-year window — small-scale, closer to a Reg Crowdfunding tier. The other permits up to $75 million per 12-month period, in the range of Reg A+ offerings that growth-stage startups use today. Issuers using either exemption still owe investors principles-based narrative disclosures, and larger offerings under the $75 million tier owe actual financial statements and ongoing reporting — this isn't a disclosure-free pass, just a lighter one. The more structurally important piece is a conditional safe harbor: under specific conditions, a crypto asset can be deemed outside the "investment contract" definition that has driven years of SEC enforcement actions against token issuers. Combined with a preemption clause waiving state securities registration requirements for qualifying offerings and certain secondary transactions, the practical effect is a project that follows the safe harbor's conditions doesn't have to fight fifty separate state regulators on top of the SEC. "Onshore innovation" SEC Chairman Paul Atkins framed the proposal as giving "crypto asset entrepreneurs and market participants clear pathways to raise capital," while preserving investor protections, and described it as part of a broader strategy to "onshore innovation in crypto asset markets" — regulatory shorthand for keeping token projects incorporating and building in the U.S. rather than Switzerland, Singapore, or the UAE. It's the same competitive framing that's shown up in the CFTC's own market-structure proposal , sent to the White House for review the same month Congress stalled. title: FinCEN Just Put a Number on Crypto Scam Losses: $13 Billion
description: FinCEN found almost $13 billion linked to crypto investment scams across all 50 states — far more than 2026's on-chain hacks have cost combined.
excerpt: On September 3, the Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network published an analysis with a number that deserves more attention than it got: nearly $13 billion in financial activity tied to suspected digital-asset investment scams, drawn from 33,904 Bank Secrecy Act reports filed by U.S. financial institutions between September 2023 and the end of 2025. The activity touched all 50 states and several U.S. territories. It's worth sitting with what this number is, and isn't. It's not a hack. Nothing here involves a smart-contract exploit, a bridge vulnerability, or a hardware-wallet firmware bug — the categories that dominate ChainBrief's security coverage and most crypto headlines generally. This is people being deceived by other people, at a scale that dwarfs the technical failures. The playbook FinCEN's report groups the activity into three overlapping scam types: "pig butchering" schemes, where a scammer builds a long-term relationship (often romantic) before introducing a fraudulent investment platform; "romance baiting," the relationship-first variant; and more generic cryptocurrency confidence schemes. The common mechanism across all three is a fake persona and sustained social engineering, aimed at getting a victim to move funds into wallets or platforms controlled by the scammer — often gradually, with fabricated "returns" shown along the way to encourage larger transfers. Why the scale matters more than any single case Compare FinCEN's roughly $13 billion figure to the crypto industry's own hack-loss tracking: researchers estimate 2026's on-chain exploits — everything from DeFi protocol bugs to the year's highest-profile hardware wallet and sidechain incidents — at around $2.2 billion year to date. Scam losses aren't a rounding error next to hack losses; they're roughly six times larger. That's a hard reframe for an industry whose security conversation is dominated by audits, bug bounties, and multisig setups — all of which do essentially nothing against a scammer who convinces someone to send funds voluntarily. title: The Race for a Federal Crypto Bank Charter Is Quietly Ending
description: Circle, Ripple, Paxos, BitGo, and Crypto.com have all won OCC national trust bank charters in 2026 — federally regulated custody, without the ability to take deposits.
excerpt: Eighteen firms applied to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency for a national trust bank charter in 2025. More than half a dozen have now cleared at least conditional approval, and the highest-profile one, Circle, has already crossed the finish line — a pattern that's turned what used to be a niche regulatory filing into 2026's clearest signal of who the federal government considers a legitimate crypto custodian. What a trust charter actually gets you A national trust bank charter is a specific, limited thing: it lets a company custody assets under federal oversight, but it does not let that company take deposits or make loans like a commercial bank. For Crypto.com, which received conditional approval in February 2026 roughly four months after applying, the charter authorizes custody and staking of digital assets and the handling of trade settlement — the CEO called it "a major step closer to meeting leading institutions' needs for a qualified custodian under federal oversight." Circle went further. On July 10, the company received final OCC approval to establish Circle National Trust, making it one of the first crypto-native firms to hold a completed national trust charter rather than a conditional one. The charter lets Circle offer fiduciary digital asset custody to institutional clients — banks, asset managers, other financial institutions — and sets up a path for USDC's own reserves to eventually be managed under the same federal trust structure. CEO Jeremy Allaire put it plainly: "Federal oversight of our trust bank sets a new standard for transparency, governance, and scale for Circle's infrastructure," adding that it "unlocks a new phase of adoption, where leading financial institutions can build on public blockchains with clarity and confidence." Who else is in the queue Circle, Ripple, and Paxos received conditional approvals in December 2025, alongside custody specialists BitGo and Fidelity Digital Assets. Bridge followed in early February 2026. One applicant, Erebor Bank, was approved for a full national bank charter rather than a trust charter — a materially different, and harder to get, designation that does permit deposits and lending. Mercury, Bunq, Nubank, World Liberty Financial, and Laser Digital are all still working through the pipeline. Why this is a market-structure story, not just a compliance story A federal trust charter answers a question institutional allocators have been asking for years: who is actually allowed to hold this on our behalf under the same regulatory umbrella as the rest of our custody relationships? title: Wall Street's Biggest Futures Exchange Now Trades Crypto Like Crypto
description: CME Group's crypto futures and options now trade 24/7 — closing the weekend gap that has separated regulated derivatives from crypto-native exchanges.
excerpt: Since May 29, CME Group's cryptocurrency futures and options have traded continuously — 24 hours a day, seven days a week, with only a two-hour weekly maintenance window. It's a small operational detail with an ironic backstory: for years, one of the most-cited critiques of crypto markets was that they never close, making them harder to regulate and easier to manipulate overnight. Now the largest regulated derivatives exchange in the world has decided that's actually the format worth copying. The gap this closes Crypto-native exchanges have run 24/7/365 since the beginning — there's no bell to open or close a market for an asset that trades globally with no single home exchange. CME's futures and options, by contrast, ran on a schedule closer to traditional derivatives: open through the week, closed for the weekend. That gap meant a trader hedging bitcoin exposure through CME carried unhedged weekend risk that a trader using a crypto-native perpetual-futures venue simply didn't. Trading now begins each week Friday at 4:00 p.m. Central on CME Globex, and weekend or holiday trades are recorded under the following business day's trade date for clearing and settlement purposes — a bookkeeping detail that still preserves standard settlement mechanics even though the market itself never technically shuts. The numbers behind the decision Tim McCourt, CME Group's Global Head of Equities, FX and Alternative Products, tied the move directly to demand: "Client demand for risk management in the digital asset market is at an all-time high, driving a record $3 trillion in notional volume across our Cryptocurrency futures and options in 2025." That's the kind of volume that turns a scheduling gap from a minor inconvenience into a competitive liability — institutional desks running real risk books don't want to be unhedged for 60-plus hours every week just because the exchange they're required to use for regulatory or compliance reasons happens to be closed. Traditional finance is catching up to crypto, not the other way around This isn't happening in isolation. Nasdaq has confirmed a nearly 23-hour trading day for U.S. equities launching in December, leaving stocks closed for just one hour out of every 24. Between that and CME's move, 2026 is turning into the year traditional market structure quietly adopts the always-on assumption crypto markets have operated under from day one — a rare instance of crypto's own design constraints becoming the model other asset classes converge toward, rather than the other way around. title: What 15 of the World's Biggest Investors Actually Think About Crypto
description: Bitwise's first institutional crypto report: 15 major investors held or added to Bitcoin through a 50% drawdown, and none cited price as a reason to sell.
excerpt: Most of what gets published about institutional crypto adoption is inferred — ETF flow data, 13F filings, secondhand reporting. On September 23, Bitwise published something different: direct interviews with 15 of the world's largest institutional allocators — endowments, foundations, public pension funds, multi-family offices, investment consultants, sovereign wealth funds, and public companies — about how they actually think about the asset class, not just what their filings show. Modest, and not moving The headline allocation number is unglamorous: most institutions surveyed hold between 1% and 2% of investable assets in crypto, with a wider range across the group of 0.5% to 13%. Every single institution interviewed owns Bitcoin, and for all of them it's the largest and longest-held crypto position — increasingly paired with gold in the same allocation bucket, treated as a similar kind of hedge rather than a growth trade. Ethereum and Solana show up too, but in smaller positions, held for shorter time horizons, and with explicit conditions attached for when the institution would exit. The drawdown nobody sold into The most striking finding is behavioral. Crypto fell by roughly 50% between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the second quarter of 2026 — a real, painful drawdown by any standard. None of the institutions Bitwise interviewed reduced their allocations during it. Several increased their positions instead. When asked what would actually trigger a sale, the answers clustered around thesis failure, a regulatory reversal, or an industry-wide credibility crisis — not price. Not one institution cited the price drop itself as a reason to consider selling. Bitwise's own framing of the finding is worth quoting directly: "The common assumption is that institutions are the weak hands in a crypto drawdown. These interviews suggest the opposite." The report also found an inverse relationship between allocation size and internal approval friction — family offices, which typically face the least internal bureaucracy, held the largest allocations in the sample, while sovereign wealth funds, which face the most committees and mandates, held the smallest. Read the sample size honestly Fifteen institutions is a real, direct-interview sample — a meaningfully different kind of evidence than survey aggregation — but it's still fifteen. title: Consumers Will Use Stablecoins — If They Feel Like a Bank Account
description: Visa's survey found stablecoin adoption intent rises from 36% to 56% with bank-level fraud protection and deposit insurance added.
excerpt: Visa's "Money Travels 2026" study, conducted by Morning Consult and published September 23, surveyed 2,192 U.S. adults between February 24 and March 2 — and the topline number cuts against a lot of crypto-industry assumptions about what's actually holding stablecoin adoption back. It isn't awareness, and it isn't the technology. It's trust in what happens if something goes wrong. Respondents were given plain-language definitions of stablecoins and related terms before answering, which matters given that 56% of them said they'd never encountered stablecoins before taking the survey. Baseline adoption intent — willingness to actually use one — sat at 36%. Add a hypothetical combination of bank-level fraud protection and deposit insurance, and that number jumped to 56%. Simply offering the stablecoin through an existing, trusted financial provider rather than a crypto-native app moved intent to 45% on its own. Trust in the wrapper, not the ledger Perhaps the most telling number in the whole survey: 64% of respondents said their trust in a payment provider mattered more to them than their confidence in the underlying technology. For an industry that spends enormous energy explaining blockchain mechanics — how reserves are held, how transactions settle, why a particular chain is more decentralized or efficient than another — that's a blunt signal that most prospective users aren't evaluating the technology at all. They're evaluating whether the institution putting its name on the product is one they already trust. Why this lands right after the Fed's rulemaking This survey result arrives in the same week as the Federal Reserve's proposed capital and redemption rules for GENIUS Act stablecoin issuers — rules that exist specifically to make "bank-level protections" something regulators can actually enforce, rather than a marketing phrase. If Visa's data is right that protections, not blockchain mechanics, are the adoption lever that matters, then the unglamorous regulatory plumbing — capital requirements, two-day redemption guarantees, reserve audits — may end up doing more for mainstream stablecoin adoption than any consumer-facing feature a wallet or app could ship. title: AI Agents Are Starting to Pay Each Other in Stablecoins
description: AI agents are settling payments to each other in stablecoins via new protocols like x402 — machine-to-machine commerce with no human approving each transaction.
excerpt: Give an AI agent a goal, a set of tools, and a budget, and it can now do something that sounds small but breaks a lot of assumptions baked into how payments work: it can pay for things on its own, without a human clicking approve. Renewing a subscription, rebalancing a treasury position in response to a market move, paying a contractor the moment a task is verified complete — all of it can now happen autonomously. And increasingly, the currency it happens in is a stablecoin, not a card network or a bank rail. This is already running, not hypothetical The clearest existing example is Polymarket, where automated trading bots have identified mispriced prediction-market contracts fast enough to earn an estimated $40 million a year across a platform that's processed more than $9 billion in total volume — a scale of machine-driven activity human traders simply can't match on speed. Audius, the decentralized music platform, routes 90% of artist earnings directly to creators in real time as content gets consumed, eliminating the monthly payout cycle that platforms like Spotify still run on. And a newer category — compliance agents — now monitors transaction flows, flags anomalies, and generates regulatory reports without a human reviewing every flagged event first. The protocol making it work: x402 The technical backbone for a lot of this is x402, which revives a dormant piece of the HTTP standard — status code 402, "Payment Required" — and turns it into functional payment infrastructure. The flow is simple: a client (often an AI agent) requests a resource, the server responds with payment terms instead of the resource itself, the client pays, a facilitator handles settlement, and the resource gets released. No account creation, no stored card number, no human checkout flow — just a machine-readable price and an instant settlement. By the end of 2025, x402 had processed more than 100 million payments, representing roughly $600 million in annualized volume, with the majority of that transaction volume running on Solana. Why stablecoins specifically Card rails were built around human-paced checkout — a person deciding to buy something, entering details, waiting a few seconds. They were never built for a server responding to a machine request thousands of times a second, each one needing instant, final settlement with no chargeback window. Stablecoins solve the specific problem agentic commerce has: a settlement asset that's fast, predictable in value, and programmable enough for a server or facilitator to release a resource the instant payment clears. title: A Five-Year-Old Bug Just Cost Bitcoin Holders $116 Million
description: A 2021 firmware flaw in Coldcard hardware wallets weakened key randomness for years, letting an attacker steal roughly $116 million from over 5,200 addresses.
excerpt: The whole point of a hardware wallet is that it generates your private key using real, physical randomness — noise from a dedicated chip that no attacker can predict or reproduce. Coinkite's Coldcard, a well-regarded hardware wallet among serious Bitcoin holders, had a firmware build error starting in March 2021 that quietly broke exactly that guarantee. It took until this past summer for anyone to notice, and by the time it was caught, an attacker had already stolen roughly $116 million. What actually broke The root cause was a single build configuration flag, MICROPY_HW_ENABLE_RNG, set to zero in firmware version 4.0.1. That flag change caused the wallet's seed-generation code to incorrectly assume hardware randomness wasn't available, and fall back to a weak software pseudorandom generator seeded only from the device's chip serial number and internal timer state — both of which are far more predictable than genuine hardware noise. The practical effect was a collapse in entropy: from a theoretical 128 bits down to as little as 40 bits on Mk3 devices, and around 72 bits on newer Mk4, Mk5, and Q models. At 40 bits of entropy, roughly a trillion possible seeds can be enumerated by a modern GPU cluster in a matter of hours — not the millions of years a properly generated key would require. How the theft actually happened The attacks began July 30 and came in four documented waves, hitting more than 5,200 addresses. The first wave alone moved roughly 594 BTC — about $38 million at the time — in just 25 minutes, a pace that only makes sense if the attacker had already pre-computed which weak seeds corresponded to funded wallets before striking. By the time all four waves were tallied, the total came to approximately 1,816 BTC, worth about $116 million. The nuance that matters for anyone who owns a Coldcard A firmware patch fixes the bug going forward, but it does nothing to protect a seed that was already generated on the flawed firmware — the weakness lives in the seed itself, not in the device running it today. Anyone who generated a Coldcard seed between March 2021 and whenever they applied the fix should treat that seed as compromised and move funds to a newly generated wallet, full stop. title: Crypto Hacks Hit a Record in 2026 — the Losses Didn't
description: 2026 crypto hack losses hit $2.2B across 288 attacks — but a small number of huge breaches, not typical exploits, account for most of the money lost.
excerpt: Add up every reported crypto hack in 2026 through late September and you get two numbers that don't seem like they should go together: 288 incidents, and roughly $2.21 billion in total losses. The attack count is a record. The dollar total, measured against how bad 2025 was, is not — and the gap between those two facts is one of the more useful ways to understand where crypto security actually stands right now. More attacks, smaller checks The first half of 2026 alone saw 207 hacks, compared with 83 in the first half of 2025 — attack frequency roughly two and a half times higher. Yet total H1 2026 losses came in at about $972 million, down from roughly $2.3 billion in the same period a year earlier. The median incident in H1 2026 involved about $219,000 — a real loss for whoever it happened to, but nowhere near headline-making. The mean, by contrast, was $4.7 million. That enormous gap between the median and the mean is the whole story: a large number of small, contained incidents are pulling the average loss size way down, while a small number of enormous ones are still doing almost all of the real financial damage. The 4-percent problem Put a number on that concentration and it's stark: roughly 4% of 2026's attacks accounted for about 75% of all stolen funds. April was one of the worst stretches, when breaches at Drift and KelpDAO together cost roughly $577 million. September added two more entries to that short, expensive list. The Liquid Network sidechain exploit drained roughly $320 million through a caching bug before about 85% was returned, and the Coldcard hardware-wallet firmware flaw cost self-custody Bitcoin holders another $116 million through a five-year-old entropy bug. Neither was a typical DeFi exploit — one was sidechain infrastructure, the other was a single hardware vendor's firmware build error. What's actually improving, and what isn't The frequency-versus-severity split suggests crypto security is genuinely getting better at the things it's had years of practice defending: routine smart-contract exploits, common reentrancy and price-oracle bugs, the kind of attack surface that's been audited, bug-bountied, and patched repeatedly across the industry. What isn't improving nearly as fast is resilience against structural, single-point-of-failure risk — a sidechain's validation logic, one vendor's firmware supply chain, a bridge's multisig configuration.
